(If your work is more suitable for medRxiv, you will need to post the preprint yourself, as the mechanisms for us to do so are still in development.)

Summary:

Coding of sound location is thought to occur in the medial (MSO) and lateral superior olivary (LSO) nuclei, with the former devoted to interaural temporal cues and the latter devoted to level difference cues. The current study shows this dichotomy is too simplistic. The authors made whole cell recordings in vivo from principal cells of the LSO and show sensitivity to transient time difference stimuli. They revealed the basis of that sensitivity, which is the convergence of excitatory synaptic events with well-timed synaptic inhibition. The reviewers were unanimously enthusiastic about the data on the responses of the LSO to transient stimuli, and the important differences in the principal and non-principal LSO cell populations. In a second section, the authors used brain slice recordings to mimic the in vivo work by stimulating excitatory and inhibitory inputs. When they could not reproduce the in vivo findings by injecting inhibitory conductances through their electrode into the soma, they speculated that the inhibition is not somatic but axonal. In anatomical work, they provided some evidence for such axonal inhibition.

Essential revisions:

The in vitro work was not as compelling as the in vivo work. One issue was that the assumptions that went into setting up the experimental paradigm were not as clearly stated and justified for the in vitro experiments. Further, the anatomical work was also not quantitative, so it was hard to know if the axonal synapses were in fact responsible for the physiological results. We propose that you either remove the in vitro and anatomical section or provide more detail for that work so that the point you are trying to make is less conjectural. We prefer the second option.

(1) The reviewers' major concern relates to your hypothesis that inhibitory synapses on the axon initial segment provide a super-fast elevation of the threshold at the spike generation region.

We like the hypothesis but are not completely convinced. We suggest that you clarify the in vitro dynamic clamp assumptions and caveats, and quantify the anatomical observations. We agree that new benchwork is undesirable, but you might have existing data that would help. We favor the idea of a model that can be accomplished remotely. There's a published two-compartment model (AIS + soma/dendrite) that you could co-opt (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30830905/).

Please add more detail on your choices of stimuli and on other aspects of the methods. In our view of your results, when you could not reproduce the in vivo findings by injecting inhibitory conductances through the electrode into the soma, you hypothesized that inhibition is not somatic but axonal. Nevertheless, the in vitro work was not as compelling as the in vivo work. The contrast between dynamic clamp of IPSPs with synaptically evoked IPSPs and their relative ability to mediate 'ITD' sensitivity is absolutely key (in your rationale) to the claim that AIS inhibition is what endows the system with its impressive behavior. You found that injection of somatic conductances were unable to shunt the EPSPs sufficiently, whereas the synapse was able to do so quite well. That, combined with the observation that inhibitory boutons are found on the AIS, is the meat of your argument. But there are problems: First, the dynamic clamp essentially reports a negative result, failure to mimic the synapse. This forces the reader to wonder if you went about it right. The methods share little about how you chose the conductance values and time course. Nothing is cited and details are sparse. You wrote that you tuned it up to get a certain size of IPSP, but how do we know if that is the right metric? Perhaps you were comparing the IPSPs to those reported in vivo. But here is another problem: we are not sure if you can compare in vitro and in vivo recordings in a quantitative way. in vitro, we see a certain resting potential of around -60 mV and overshooting spikes. in vivo, the resting potentials are hidden, and the traces all baselined to zero. The spikes are small. We do not know how the input resistances compare. Thus, the size of the IPSP is not a reliable metric for matching in vivo and in vitro, as little else matches. Another mystery is how the strength of the synaptic events was set, and how they are compared to the dynamic clamp IPSPs. A better approach would have been to measure the effective synaptic IPSC in voltage clamp in order to determine the conductance and the waveform, then use that to set the dynamic clamp values. With respect to the dynamic clamp, would there be some relationship between the ability of dynamic clamp IPSGs to block spikes and the distance of the recording electrode to the AIS? Were reconstructions obtained for the relatively effective cases (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D, bottom right)?

We note that the discussion hardly mentions the AIS work, suggesting that you may also not be that comfortable with your hypothesis. Furthermore, the anatomical work too was not quantitative, so it is hard to know if the axonal synapses were in fact responsible for the physiological results. Another concern related to the AIS anatomy is that it is hard to tell why LSO neurons are so heavily encrusted with inhibitory synapses if the ones that matter are a few boutons on the AIS.

(2) In vivo stimuli: We appreciate the detail provided, but some statements do not appear to be clearly supported by the evidence. For example, measures of ITD function half-widths are said to be narrower for LSO principal cells (lines 129-133; Figure 1K). The p value is modest and the data suggest a more nuanced interpretation. The population of LSO principal neurons is dominated by those with high CFs, and the opposite is true for MSO neurons. Furthermore, non-principal neuron half-widths are just as sharp as those of principal neurons for CFs above 4 kHz. Please clarify if this effect is due to better afferent entrainment to the higher frequency components of the click stimulus, to principal neuron biological factors, or both? Did you measure an FFT of the click stimulus? In addition, might the relatively poor performance of low CF neurons be related to non-uniform glycine receptor density, with greater levels in the medial limb (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/2890726/)?

The recorded LSO principal cells have ITD functions that are positioned outside of the relevant 120 µs ITD range for gerbils (Figure 1-figure suppl 2). We find it difficult to visualize the behaviorally-relevant contribution of the new property. The final experiment (Figure 7L and Figure 7-figure suppl 2) appears to show that ILD performance alone (ITD=0) is better than ITD performance alone (ILD=0), and when both properties are co-varied, the neurons still respond only at values that correspond to a fully lateralized stimulus position. Is this correct?

(3) The monaural suprathreshold SPL values were obtained as described in the methods (lines 788-798), but it is not always clear which SPL values were used to obtain click-evoked ITD functions (Figure 1—figure supplement 1 provides levels for tone-evoked ILDs, and Figure 2 states that the SPL was 60 dB, presumably at both ear). Please provide information about the effect of monaural sound level on the click-evoked ITD functions, including whether this factor has an impact on the relevant range of time differences. Specifically, while ILD and ITD were varied independently and together (Figure 7), was ITD ever adjusted to be appropriate for each ILD presented (i.e., within the +/- 120 µs window)? If we understand correctly, the Voronoi diagram in Figure 7K suggests that the neuron does not fire in a biologically relevant range of ILDs (=/1 15 dB) and ITDs (+/- 120 µs) for a CF of 3.5 kHz.

(4) Discussion: Please offer us a more rigorous argument about the conditions under which LSO ITD processing is used, either alone, or alongside IID processing. Specifically, we remain uncertain about the contribution of the new LSO coding property to perception. For example, we know that humans have good single-click ILD thresholds (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21117758/; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15109699/), suggesting that these are sufficient to support rapid lateralization.

You refer briefly to sounds that would take advantage of the new LSO neuron encoding attribute (e.g., ln 17: "Locomotion generates adventitious sounds…"; lines 68-69: High-frequency transients are generated as adventitious sounds created by the locomotion of animals at close range…"). The authors should provide a referenced argument about the prevalence and acoustic properties of the natural sounds that could not be lateralized from their ITDs by MSO neurons, or from their ILDs by LSO neurons. Related to this is the final conclusion (lines 716-717, "…the time-based role of LSO is the more dominant (but previously underestimated) role."). Doesn't this statement rest on the premise that brief transients are the more dominant signal? The natural acoustic world is dominated by sounds with slow envelopes, especially for vocal communication. Consider reviews like Elliott and Theunissen (2009) and Ding et al. (2017). Gerbils might spend much of their time listening to, and possibly localizing, conspecific vocalizations which tend to be modulated in the same low range (Ter-Mikaelian et al., 2012), and which will be encoded by LSO neurons using a mechanism that is not exquisitely sensitive to microsecond time differences.

claims.evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claims.claim: This study reports AIS inhibition by glycinergic neurons for the first time.
claims.source: Here, we report AIS inhibition by glycinergic neurons for the first time, with a specific functional role tying together several puzzling anatomical and physiological features.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the immunohistochemistry and EM data in Figures 5 and 6.

claims.claim: Humans are exquisitely sensitive to the spatial cues of time and intensity differences between sounds at the two ears (ITDs and IIDs).
claims.source: Humans are exquisitely sensitive to the spatial cues of time and intensity differences between sounds at the two ears (ITDs and IIDs; Klumpp and Eady, 1956; Yost and Dye, 1988).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to psychophysical studies.

claims.claim: The classic 'duplex' account posits that ITDs operate for low-frequency sounds and IIDs for high-frequency sounds.
claims.source: The classic 'duplex' account posits that these two cues operate in different frequency regions: spatial localization is subserved by ITDs for low-frequency and by IIDs for high-frequency sounds (Strutt, 1907).
claims.evidence: This is a historical account supported by a citation to Strutt, 1907.

claims.claim: The MSO generates sensitivity to ITDs.
claims.source: This account dovetails with the existence of two brainstem circuits seemingly dedicated to the extraction of these cues: the MSO generates sensitivity to ITDs (Goldberg and Brown, 1969; Yin and Chan, 1990) and the LSO to IIDs (reviewed by Tollin, 2003).
claims.evidence: This is the traditional view supported by citations.

claims.claim: The LSO generates sensitivity to IIDs.
claims.source: This account dovetails with the existence of two brainstem circuits seemingly dedicated to the extraction of these cues: the MSO generates sensitivity to ITDs (Goldberg and Brown, 1969; Yin and Chan, 1990) and the LSO to IIDs (reviewed by Tollin, 2003).
claims.evidence: This is the traditional view supported by a citation.

claims.claim: MSO neurons perform coincidence detection on excitatory spike trains from both ears.
claims.source: These two circuits share many components: their most salient difference is that MSO neurons perform coincidence detection on the excitatory spike trains they receive from both ears, while LSO neurons perform a differencing operation comparing net excitatory input from the ipsilateral vs. net inhibitory input from the contralateral ear.
claims.evidence: This is a description of MSO function supported by general knowledge in the field.

claims.claim: LSO neurons perform a differencing operation comparing net excitatory input from the ipsilateral vs. net inhibitory input from the contralateral ear.
claims.source: These two circuits share many components: their most salient difference is that MSO neurons perform coincidence detection on the excitatory spike trains they receive from both ears, while LSO neurons perform a differencing operation comparing net excitatory input from the ipsilateral vs. net inhibitory input from the contralateral ear.
claims.evidence: This is a description of LSO function supported by general knowledge in the field.

claims.claim: The classical duplex account does not square with striking physiological and morphological features found in the circuits converging on the LSO.
claims.source: This classical duplex account of the respective role of these two binaural nuclei does not square with striking physiological and morphological features found in the circuits converging on the LSO, including some of the largest synapses in the brain (e.g. the calyx of Held).
claims.evidence: This is an argument based on inference from known anatomical features.

claims.claim: The LSO circuit includes some of the largest synapses in the brain (e.g. the calyx of Held).
claims.source: This classical duplex account of the respective role of these two binaural nuclei does not square with striking physiological and morphological features found in the circuits converging on the LSO, including some of the largest synapses in the brain (e.g. the calyx of Held).
claims.evidence: This is a well-known anatomical fact.

claims.claim: The LSO is specialized for temporal comparisons between the two ears.
claims.source: This and other observations suggest that the LSO is not simply weighing excitation vs. inhibition toward IID-sensitivity, but is specialized for temporal comparisons between the two ears.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by inference from anatomical and physiological observations.

claims.claim: Many studies observed ITD-sensitivity of LSO neurons to a range of sounds (tones, amplitude-modulated tones, noise).
claims.source: Many studies indeed observed ITD-sensitivity of LSO neurons to a range of sounds (tones, amplitude-modulated tones, noise [Caird and Klinke, 1983; Irvine et al., 2001; Joris, 1996; Joris and Yin, 1995; Tollin and Yin, 2005]), but ITD-sensitivity to these sounds was weak compared to the effects of IIDs and not commensurate with the striking specializations of the LSO circuit (Joris and Yin, 1998).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: ITD-sensitivity of LSO neurons to tones, amplitude-modulated tones, and noise was weak compared to the effects of IIDs.
claims.source: Many studies indeed observed ITD-sensitivity of LSO neurons to a range of sounds (tones, amplitude-modulated tones, noise [Caird and Klinke, 1983; Irvine et al., 2001; Joris, 1996; Joris and Yin, 1995; Tollin and Yin, 2005]), but ITD-sensitivity to these sounds was weak compared to the effects of IIDs and not commensurate with the striking specializations of the LSO circuit (Joris and Yin, 1998).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Strong ITD-sensitivity in LSO neurons was occasionally observed to electrical shocks in vitro.
claims.source: The only stimuli to which strong ITD-sensitivity was occasionally observed in LSO neurons was to electrical shocks in vitro (Sanes, 1990; Wu and Kelly, 1992) and, in vivo, to brisk changes in sound characteristics, usually referred to as 'transients'.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Strong ITD-sensitivity in LSO neurons was occasionally observed in vivo to brisk changes in sound characteristics (transients).
claims.source: The only stimuli to which strong ITD-sensitivity was occasionally observed in LSO neurons was to electrical shocks in vitro (Sanes, 1990; Wu and Kelly, 1992) and, in vivo, to brisk changes in sound characteristics, usually referred to as 'transients'.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Examples of transients are clicks, tone onsets, and fast frequency-modulated sweeps.
claims.source: Examples of such transients are clicks, tone onsets, and fast frequency-modulated sweeps (Caird and Klinke, 1983; Irvine et al., 2001; Joris and Yin, 1995; Park et al., 1996).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: High-frequency transients are generated as adventitious sounds created by the locomotion of predators or prey at close range.
claims.source: High-frequency transients are generated as adventitious sounds created by the locomotion of predators or prey at close range (Clark, 2016; Goerlitz and Siemers, 2007).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Behavioral experiments show that lemurs rely on adventitious sounds to forage.
claims.source: Behavioral experiments show that lemurs rely on such sounds to forage (Siemers et al., 2007), and mice choose routes to minimize the generation of such sounds (Roche et al., 1999).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Siemers et al., 2007.

claims.claim: Mice choose routes to minimize the generation of adventitious sounds.
claims.source: Behavioral experiments show that lemurs rely on such sounds to forage (Siemers et al., 2007), and mice choose routes to minimize the generation of such sounds (Roche et al., 1999).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Roche et al., 1999.

claims.claim: Detection and lateralization of adventitious sounds was a strong evolutionary pressure for the high-frequency LSO circuit and drove its striking temporal specializations.
claims.source: This leads to the hypothesis that detection and lateralization of these sounds was a strong evolutionary pressure for this high-frequency circuit and drove its striking temporal specializations (Joris and Trussell, 2018).
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by a citation and inference from behavioral and anatomical data.

claims.claim: LSO principal cells have fast membrane properties and respond transiently to tones.
claims.source: The recent discovery that LSO principal cells have fast membrane properties and respond transiently to tones (Franken et al., 2018) gives extra weight to the importance of timing in this circuit.
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Franken et al., 2018.

claims.claim: In vivo whole-cell patch clamp recordings were obtained from 19 LSO neurons and 11 MSO neurons while presenting clicks at different ITDs.
claims.source: We obtained in vivo whole-cell recordings while presenting clicks at different ITDs in 19 LSO neurons and 11 MSO neurons.
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental methods and sample size.

claims.claim: Responses to tones for the recorded cells have been reported before.
claims.source: Responses to tones for these cells have been reported before (Franken et al., 2018; Franken et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous publications.

claims.claim: Sharp sensitivity to ITDs of clicks was found in LSO but not MSO neurons.
claims.source: We were surprised to find sharp sensitivity to ITDs of clicks in LSO but not MSO neurons.
claims.evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1.

claims.claim: A principal LSO neuron showed a U-shaped ITD tuning function with extraordinarily steep slopes (−6.5 and 4.2 spikes per click/ms).
claims.source: Figure 1A shows sensitivity to ITDs of transients in a principal LSO neuron (IID function in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A). Identical impulsive sounds ('clicks') were delivered to the two ears with varying ITD. The neuron reliably fires a single spike at large negative and positive ITDs, but is completely inhibited over a sub-millisecond range near 0 μs. The resulting U-shaped tuning function has extraordinarily steep slopes (−6.5 and 4.2 spikes per click/ms); a narrow and deep trough (450 μs halfwidth) with complete suppression of spiking, and low variability.
claims.evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 1A with quantitative measurements.

claims.claim: The principal LSO neuron's ITD tuning function had a narrow and deep trough (450 μs halfwidth) with complete suppression of spiking.
claims.source: The resulting U-shaped tuning function has extraordinarily steep slopes (−6.5 and 4.2 spikes per click/ms); a narrow and deep trough (450 μs halfwidth) with complete suppression of spiking, and low variability.
claims.evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 1A with quantitative measurements.

claims.claim: The principal LSO neuron's ITD tuning had an ITD-SNR value of 0.86.
claims.source: A measure of tuning, ITD-SNR (the ITD-dependent variance in spike rate divided by the total variance [Hancock et al., 2010]) gives a value of 0.86.
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative measure calculated from the data in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: At large negative ITDs, when the ipsilateral (excitatory) ear is leading, excitation is unopposed and reliably triggers a single spike in the principal LSO neuron.
claims.source: At large negative click ITDs, when the ipsilateral (excitatory) ear is leading, excitation is unopposed and reliably triggers a single spike.
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B waterfall plot.

claims.claim: At large positive ITDs, the leading contralateral (inhibitory ear) click is not able to suppress spiking to the lagging ipsilateral click in the principal LSO neuron, even for lags between IPSP and EPSP as small as 0.25 ms.
claims.source: Likewise, at large positive ITDs, the leading contralateral (inhibitory ear) click is not able to suppress spiking to the lagging ipsilateral click, even for lags between IPSP and EPSP as small as 0.25 ms.
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B waterfall plot.

claims.claim: A non-principal LSO neuron showed ITD tuning with shallower slopes (−1.0 and 2.0 spikes per click/ms), wider trough (halfwidth 1350 μs), and higher variability, yielding an ITD-SNR of 0.63.
claims.source: Figure 1C and D show data for a non-principal LSO neuron (IID function in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B): here the intracellular traces are more complex than a stimulus-like stacking of PSPs, but nevertheless tuning to ITDs is present, be it with shallower slopes (−1.0 and 2.0 spikes per click/ms), wider trough (halfwidth 1350 μs), and higher variability, yielding an ITD-SNR of 0.63.
claims.evidence: This is directly shown in Figures 1C and 1D with quantitative measurements.

claims.claim: An MSO neuron showed an excitatory peak near 0 ms ITD with one of the steepest-sloped ITD-functions of the MSO sample (2.1 spikes per click/ms for slope at ITD <0 ms), but the ITD-tuning lacked the acuity observed in principal LSO cells, with an ITD-SNR of only 0.38.
claims.source: Figure 1E and F show data for an MSO neuron. As expected, the main feature in the response is an excitatory peak near 0 ms. Even though this is one of the steepest-sloped ITD-functions of our MSO sample (2.1 spikes per click/ms for slope at ITD <0 ms), the ITD-tuning lacks the acuity observed in principal LSO cells, with an ITD-SNR of only 0.38.
claims.evidence: This is directly shown in Figures 1E and 1F with quantitative measurements.

claims.claim: Spiking in the MSO neuron is not restricted to ITDs where the two events coincide, but also occurs at other ITDs, where the click at either ear can elicit a suprathreshold response.
claims.source: The intracellular data (Figure 1F) reveal that, surprisingly, spiking is not restricted to ITDs where the two events coincide, but also occurs at other ITDs, where the click at either ear can elicit a suprathreshold response.
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 1F intracellular recordings.

claims.claim: LSO neurons were sorted into principal and non-principal neurons based on anatomical and physiological criteria.
claims.source: LSO neurons were sorted into principal and non-principal neurons based on anatomical and physiological criteria (Franken et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This describes the classification method with a citation to previous work.

claims.claim: In principal LSO cells, the spiking output of most cells is steeply dependent on ITD at some ITD range.
claims.source: In principal cells (Figure 1G), the spiking output of most cells is steeply dependent on ITD at some ITD range.
claims.evidence: This is shown in the population data in Figure 1G.

claims.claim: Non-principal LSO neuron tuning is much more varied but occasionally also features steep slopes.
claims.source: Non-principal LSO neuron tuning (Figure 1H) is much more varied but occasionally also features steep slopes.
claims.evidence: This is shown in the population data in Figure 1H.

claims.claim: Steeper slopes and narrower ITD functions were observed at higher sound levels in LSO neurons.
claims.source: We observed steeper slopes and narrower functions at higher sound levels (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A,B).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A,B.

claims.claim: ITD-tuning was surprisingly weak in the majority of MSO neurons.
claims.source: Compared to LSO, ITD-tuning was surprisingly weak in the majority of MSO neurons (Figure 1I).
claims.evidence: This is shown in the population data in Figure 1I.

claims.claim: Halfwidths of the ITD-tuning functions are smaller for principal LSO cells than for MSO cells (respective median (IQR) 0.84 ms (0.48), 8 cells, and 1.40 ms (0.74), 6 cells; Mann-Whitney U = 40.0, p=0.043; θ = 0.83 (95% CI [0.52, 0.95])).
claims.source: Halfwidths of the ITD-tuning functions, that is the ITD range over which the response is suppressed by ≥50% (for LSO), or enhanced by ≥50% (for MSO), are smaller for principal LSO cells than for MSO cells (Figure 1K; respective median (IQR) 0.84 ms (0.48), 8 cells, and 1.40 ms (0.74), 6 cells; Mann-Whitney U = 40.0, p=0.043; θ = 0.83 (95% CI [0.52, 0.95])).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical comparison of data shown in Figure 1K.

claims.claim: Halfwidth is smaller for higher log(CF) (computed across LSO and MSO cells: r = −0.62, p=0.001).
claims.source: Halfwidth is smaller for higher log(CF) (computed across LSO and MSO cells: r = −0.62, p=0.001), potentially due to the non-uniform distribution of glycine receptors with higher concentrations in the high-frequency region (Sanes et al., 1987) and wider bandwidth at high CFs.
claims.evidence: This is a correlation analysis with a proposed mechanistic explanation supported by a citation.

claims.claim: There was no significant difference in CF for the principal LSO and MSO neurons included in the ITD-SNR analysis (Mann-Whitney U = 31.0, p=0.46).
claims.source: there was no significant difference in CF for the principal LSO and MSO neurons included in this analysis (Mann-Whitney U = 31.0, p=0.46).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical test showing no difference in a potential confounding variable.

claims.claim: ITD-SNR is significantly higher for principal LSO cells than for non-principal LSO cells (non-principal LSO: median (IQR) 0.33 (0.31), 9 cells; Mann-Whitney U = 54.0, p=0.016; θ = 0.86 (95% CI [0.57, 0.96])).
claims.source: We also find a significantly higher ITD-SNR for principal LSO cells than for non-principal LSO cells (non-principal LSO: median (IQR) 0.33 (0.31), 9 cells; Mann-Whitney U = 54.0, p=0.016; θ = 0.86 (95% CI [0.57, 0.96])).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical comparison.

claims.claim: The difference in ITD-SNR between principal and non-principal LSO cells is not explained by differences in sound level.
claims.source: This is not explained by differences in sound level (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C,D).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3C,D.

claims.claim: LSO neurons receive a well-timed EPSP in response to monaural ipsilateral clicks, which reliably trigger spikes.
claims.source: As illustrated for two LSO neurons (Figure 2A and B), they receive a well-timed EPSP in response to monaural ipsilateral clicks, which reliably trigger spikes, and a well-timed IPSP in response to monaural contralateral clicks.
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A and B intracellular recordings.

claims.claim: LSO neurons receive a well-timed IPSP in response to monaural contralateral clicks.
claims.source: As illustrated for two LSO neurons (Figure 2A and B), they receive a well-timed EPSP in response to monaural ipsilateral clicks, which reliably trigger spikes, and a well-timed IPSP in response to monaural contralateral clicks.
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A and B intracellular recordings.

claims.claim: Tuning curves centered at negative ITDs suggest that contralateral inhibition effectively has a shorter latency (by a few hundred microseconds) than ipsilateral excitation.
claims.source: For example, tuning curves centered at negative ITDs (Figures 1A and 2D) suggest that contralateral inhibition effectively has a shorter latency (by a few hundred microseconds) than ipsilateral excitation, while the opposite is the case when centered at positive ITDs (Figures 1C and 8L).
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the ITD tuning curves shown in the figures.

claims.claim: Intracellular records show that the latencies of EPSPs and IPSPs are closely matched in LSO neurons, for both principal and non-principal neurons, with the IPSP sometimes arriving first.
claims.source: Our intracellular records allow direct measurement and show that indeed the latencies are closely matched, for both principal and non-principal neurons, with the IPSP sometimes arriving first (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C comparing ipsilateral and contralateral latencies.

claims.claim: In eight principal LSO neurons, a small positive deflection was observed preceding the IPSP by ~0.5 ms.
claims.source: In eight principal neurons, we observed a small positive deflection preceding the IPSP by ~0.5 ms (arrowhead and insert Figure 2A, see also Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), suggesting that consistent, precise response timing is already present at the presynaptic level.
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A, 2F, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: The small positive deflection preceding the IPSP suggests that consistent, precise response timing is already present at the presynaptic level.
claims.source: In eight principal neurons, we observed a small positive deflection preceding the IPSP by ~0.5 ms (arrowhead and insert Figure 2A, see also Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), suggesting that consistent, precise response timing is already present at the presynaptic level.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed prepotential.

claims.claim: The IPSP duration extends to almost 5 ms in principal LSO cells.
claims.source: Strikingly, the IPSP duration extends to almost 5 ms in principal cells (Figure 2A), close to an order of magnitude larger than the halfwidth of the tuning function to ITDs (Figures 1A and 2D).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: The IPSP duration is close to an order of magnitude larger than the halfwidth of the ITD tuning function in principal LSO cells.
claims.source: Strikingly, the IPSP duration extends to almost 5 ms in principal cells (Figure 2A), close to an order of magnitude larger than the halfwidth of the tuning function to ITDs (Figures 1A and 2D).
claims.evidence: This is a comparison of measurements from Figures 1A, 2A, and 2D.

claims.claim: The effective window of inhibition in LSO neurons is much smaller than the IPSP duration, consistent with in vitro data.
claims.source: This is consistent with in vitro data (Sanes, 1990; Wu and Kelly, 1992), where the effective window of inhibition was also reported to be much smaller than the IPSP duration.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous in vitro studies.

claims.claim: At large negative ITD delays, the leading EPSP reliably triggers spiking in a principal LSO neuron, unhindered by the ensuing IPSP.
claims.source: At large negative delays (Figure 2E1 and 2E2), the leading EPSP reliably triggers spiking, unhindered by the ensuing IPSP.
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 2E1 and 2E2.

claims.claim: When the IPSP leads and significantly overlaps with the EPSP in a principal LSO neuron, it fails to inhibit spiking.
claims.source: More surprisingly, when the IPSP leads and significantly overlaps with the EPSP (Figure 2E6), it also fails to inhibit spiking.
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 2E6.

claims.claim: Only when the early steep slope of the IPSP coincides with the early steep slope of the EPSP are spikes completely blocked in a principal LSO neuron.
claims.source: Only when the early steep slope of the IPSP coincides with the early steep slope of the EPSP are spikes completely blocked (Figure 2E4).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 2E4.

claims.claim: MSO neurons approach archetypal coincidence detectors.
claims.source: MSO neurons approach archetypal coincidence detectors (Joris and van der Heijden, 2019) and respond poorly to monaural stimulation and to temporally misaligned inputs (Goldberg and Brown, 1969; Yin and Chan, 1990).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: MSO neurons respond poorly to monaural stimulation and to temporally misaligned inputs.
claims.source: MSO neurons approach archetypal coincidence detectors (Joris and van der Heijden, 2019) and respond poorly to monaural stimulation and to temporally misaligned inputs (Goldberg and Brown, 1969; Yin and Chan, 1990).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Coincidence detection in MSO neurons largely failed in response to clicks because of a surprising efficacy of monaural stimuli.
claims.source: This largely failed in response to clicks, because of a surprising efficacy of monaural stimuli.
claims.evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 3A and B.

claims.claim: Depolarizing events dominate in MSO neurons in response to monaural clicks and often generate spikes.
claims.source: Figure 3A and 3B show responses to monaural ipsilateral (top panels) or contralateral (bottom panels) clicks for two MSO neurons. Depolarizing events dominate and often generate spikes.
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A and B.

claims.claim: Monaural spike rates to clicks in MSO neurons were substantial and could even equal spike rates to binaural clicks.
claims.source: Examples of spike rates as a function of click intensity (Figure 3C and 3D), illustrate that monaural spike rates to clicks were substantial and could even equal spike rates to binaural clicks (here delivered at ITD = 0 ms, generating a spike rate >90% of the peak of the click ITD function).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 3C and D.

claims.claim: MSO summation ratios in response to clicks were all <1.3 and had a median of 0.97.
claims.source: MSO summation ratios in response to clicks (Figure 3F, magenta) were all <1.3 and had a median of 0.97, indicating that the binaural response rates are similar to the sum of monaural response rates.
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 3F with statistical summary.

claims.claim: MSO summation ratios to tones were substantially higher than those to clicks (respective median (IQR) 7.56 (11.41), 23 cells and 0.97 (0.38), 5 cells; Mann-Whitney U = 4.0, p=0.001; θ = 0.03 (95% CI [0.004, 0.29])).
claims.source: In contrast, MSO summation ratios to tones were substantially higher than those to clicks (Figure 3F, black; respective median (IQR) 7.56 (11.41), 23 cells and 0.97 (0.38), 5 cells; Mann-Whitney U = 4.0, p=0.001; θ = 0.03 (95% CI [0.004, 0.29])).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical comparison of data shown in Figure 3F.

claims.claim: The binaural advantage that MSO neurons display for tones is largely non-existent for clicks.
claims.source: This convincingly shows that the binaural advantage that MSO neurons display for tones is largely non-existent for clicks.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the summation ratio data.

claims.claim: LSO responses all resulted in summation ratios well above two.
claims.source: LSO responses all resulted in summation ratios well above two (Figure 3F, green), substantially higher than for MSO responses to clicks (respectively 7 cells and 5 cells, Mann-Whitney U = 0, p=0.003; θ = 0 (95% CI [0, 0.32])).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 3F with statistical comparison.

claims.claim: Binaural summation to clicks for LSO cells clearly surpasses that of MSO cells.
claims.source: Binaural summation to clicks for LSO cells thus clearly surpasses that of MSO cells.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the summation ratio comparison.

claims.claim: In vitro experiments were performed in P19-22 gerbils.
claims.source: To better understand the narrow, sub-millisecond (Figures 1A, 1K and 2D) window of inhibition in LSO neurons, we performed in vitro experiments in P19-22 gerbils.
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental methods.

claims.claim: Shocks to LSO afferents evoke well-timed, transient inhibition and/or excitation and are a particularly apt analogue of acoustic clicks.
claims.source: Shocks to LSO afferents evoke well-timed, transient inhibition and/or excitation and are a particularly apt analogue of acoustic clicks.
claims.evidence: This is a methodological statement about the appropriateness of the in vitro stimulation method.

claims.claim: Early experiments shocking inputs on both sides showed clear ITD-sensitivity very similar to in vivo responses.
claims.source: Indeed, early experiments shocking inputs on both sides (Sanes, 1990; Wu and Kelly, 1992), and recent experiments using optogenetic stimulation (Gjoni et al., 2018b), showed clear ITD-sensitivity very similar to in vivo responses.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: When ipsilateral excitation was triggered synaptically and inhibition was simulated by injecting simulated conductances, this protocol did not result in a profound inhibitory trough in the tuning function in vitro.
claims.source: Figure 4A shows recordings from an LSO neuron where ipsilateral excitation was triggered synaptically by electrical shocks, inhibition was simulated by injecting simulated conductances, and their relative timing was varied to mimic ITDs. Surprisingly, this protocol did not result in a profound inhibitory trough in the tuning function in vitro (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A and C.

claims.claim: Although U- or V-shaped tuning functions were obtained with simulated inhibition, full inhibition (spike rate of 0 spikes/s) was not reached in most cases.
claims.source: Results for seven other neurons are shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D (solid lines): although U- or V-shaped tuning functions were obtained, full inhibition (spike rate of 0 spikes/s) was not reached in most cases.
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: ITD tuning expressed as ITD-SNR is less pronounced for in vitro functions with simulated inhibition than for in vivo functions (respective median (IQR) 0.40 (0.18), eight neurons and 0.62 (0.17), seven neurons; Mann-Whitney U = 51.0, p=0.006; θ = 0.91 (95% CI [0.62, 0.98])).
claims.source: ITD tuning expressed as ITD-SNR is less pronounced for these in vitro functions than for in vivo functions (respective median (IQR) 0.40 (0.18), eight neurons and 0.62 (0.17), seven neurons; Mann-Whitney U = 51.0, p=0.006; θ = 0.91 (95% CI [0.62, 0.98])).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical comparison.

claims.claim: Inhibition simulated by somatic injection of conductances cannot reproduce the profound inhibition observed with comparable levels of hyperpolarization in vivo.
claims.source: Thus, inhibition simulated by somatic injection of conductances cannot reproduce the profound inhibition observed with comparable levels of hyperpolarization in vivo.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of in vitro and in vivo data.

claims.claim: When natural, spatially distributed synaptic inhibition was generated by delivering shocks to contralateral inputs while excitation was simulated by conductance clamp at the soma, profound inhibition of spiking was reached in all neurons.
claims.source: To test whether the efficacy of inhibition is sensitive to the spatial location of inhibition, we reversed the stimulus protocol: we generated natural, spatially distributed synaptic inhibition by delivering shocks to contralateral inputs, while excitation was simulated by conductance clamp at the soma. Under these conditions, despite the similar range of hyperpolarization apparent at the soma, profound inhibition of spiking was reached in the neuron in Figure 4B and in all neurons.
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B and D.

claims.claim: The tuning functions with synaptically evoked inhibition were very similar to the ITD functions observed in vivo in terms of slope as well as ITD-SNR.
claims.source: The tuning functions were very similar to the ITD functions observed in vivo (Figure 4D; Figure 4—figure supplement 1E, solid lines); compare with Figures 1A, 1G and 2D, in terms of slope as well as ITD-SNR (Figure 4E, blue).

claims.claim: LSO neurons show graded latency-intensity changes.
claims.source: It has been hypothesized that temporal specializations in the LSO-circuit evolved to generate tuning to ITDs of transient sounds congruent with IID-tuning (Joris and Trussell, 2018). Classical tuning to IIDs is sigmodial (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), with higher spike output for IIDs < 0 and complete inhibition of spiking for IIDs > 0, so that LSO neurons are excited by sounds in the ipsilateral hemifield (Tollin and Yin, 2002; Figure 8A, cartoons below the abscissa illustrate the accompanying PSP changes). Congruence of ITD- and IID-tuning would be obtained if the 'left' slope of ITD-functions is centered over the ITD-range relevant to the animal (Figure 8B, function 3): an increase in firing rate would then consistently signal a sound source more toward the ipsilateral side, for both cues. Our sample (Figure 1 Figure 1—figure supplement 2), as well as published ITD-functions (Beiderbeck et al., 2018; Irvine et al., 2001; Joris and Yin, 1995; Park et al., 1996), do not support such congruency as a dominant feature: indeed for at least a sizable fraction of neurons, it is the 'right' slope that is closest to 0 ms (Figure 8B, function 1). For cases where the ITD-function is centered near 0 ms (Figure 8B, function 2, example in Figure 8L [cyan]), there is an additional issue of ambiguity: a rise in spike rate could signal both a leftward or rightward change in horizontal position of the sound source. A similar problem occurs at the population level if some neurons have the 'left' slope near 0 and others the 'right' slope. However, a natural and elegant solution to these issues is directly embedded in the properties of the LSO circuit.
claims.evidence: This is a statement introducing the analysis of latency-intensity changes.

claims.source: Figure 8D and E show how PSPs change with sound intensity for a principal and a non-principal cell. In the principal neuron, the changes in both EPSP and IPSP are extremely reproducible and finely graded in amplitude and latency with increasing SPL, also for individual trials (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A).

claims.claim: Exquisite timing in afferent inputs supplies LSO principal cells with temporally punctate events.

results.result: LSO principal neurons show exquisite ITD-sensitivity to clicks with extraordinarily steep slopes, narrow tuning functions, and high ITD-SNR values, significantly surpassing MSO neurons. Principal LSO cells exhibit U-shaped ITD tuning with complete suppression of spiking over sub-millisecond ranges, while MSO neurons show weak and variable ITD tuning to clicks.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C37-C56 provide converging evidence from in vivo whole-cell recordings (C35) showing quantitative measurements of ITD tuning in LSO and MSO neurons. The data demonstrate statistically significant differences in halfwidths (C51) and ITD-SNR (C54, C55) between principal LSO and MSO neurons, with appropriate statistical tests and effect sizes reported. The intracellular recordings (C38-C45) provide mechanistic insight into the underlying synaptic events.

results.result: LSO neurons receive well-timed EPSPs and IPSPs with closely matched latencies, but effective inhibition occurs only over an extremely short window (~0.5 ms) despite IPSP durations extending to ~5 ms. A prepotential preceding the IPSP suggests presynaptic temporal precision.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C68 and C130 are supported by direct intracellular measurements shown in Figure 2. The data demonstrate the temporal relationship between EPSPs and IPSPs (C60), the narrow effective window of inhibition (C66-C68), and the discovery of a prepotential (C61, C130). The quantitative measurements of IPSP duration (~5 ms, C63) versus effective inhibition window (~0.5 ms, C64) are directly shown in the data.

results.result: MSO neurons show poor binaural sensitivity to clicks due to strong monaural responses, with summation ratios near 1.0 for clicks compared to >7.5 for tones. LSO neurons show superior binaural summation with ratios well above 2.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C78 and C123 are supported by intracellular recordings and quantitative analysis in Figure 3. The summation ratio analysis (C74, C75, C77) includes appropriate statistical tests (Mann-Whitney U tests with effect sizes) comparing MSO responses to clicks versus tones, and LSO versus MSO responses to clicks. The data demonstrate that MSO coincidence detection fails for transient stimuli.

results.result: In vitro experiments reveal that synaptically evoked inhibition is required for profound suppression of spiking in LSO neurons. Simulated inhibition via somatic conductance or current injection produces weaker ITD tuning than synaptic inhibition, suggesting inhibitory synapses are located closer to the spike initiation zone.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C90 and C131 are supported by in vitro dynamic clamp experiments shown in Figure 4. The comparison between simulated and synaptic inhibition includes quantitative ITD-SNR measurements with statistical tests (C84, C88). The reversal experiment (C86) where excitation is simulated and inhibition is synaptic provides strong evidence for the spatial location hypothesis (C90). The same findings with current injection (C89) strengthen the conclusion.

results.result: Immunohistochemistry and electron microscopy reveal inhibitory synapses on the axon initial segment of LSO principal neurons but not MSO neurons. This represents the first report of AIS inhibition by glycinergic neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C93-C98, C15, and C132 are supported by direct anatomical evidence from immunohistochemistry (Figure 5) and electron microscopy (Figure 6). The data show gephyrin-positive puncta on the AIS (C93-C95) and synaptic profiles confirmed by EM in three LSO principal neurons (C96, C97) but not in two MSO neurons (C98). The novelty claim (C15) is supported by the anatomical evidence combined with the lack of prior reports.

results.result: Computational modeling demonstrates that inhibitory synapses on the AIS combined with somatic inhibition produce deeper ITD tuning than somatic inhibition alone. The model shows that AIS inhibition alone is insufficient, requiring cooperation with somatic inhibition.
results.evaluation: Claims C9, C99-C103, and C133 are supported by computational modeling results in Figure 7. The model systematically tests the hypothesis by comparing different inhibitory synapse arrangements (C100, C101) and shows robustness across parameter ranges (C103). The modeling provides mechanistic support for the anatomical findings and links them to the physiological observations. However, the model relies on several assumptions about coupling constants and synaptic parameters that could affect the conclusions.

results.result: LSO neurons show graded latency-intensity changes (~10-20 μs/dB) that interact with ITDs to disambiguate spatial tuning. IIDs affect both amplitude and timing of PSPs, and cue combination removes ambiguity by eliminating the right slope of ITD tuning and generating a steep left slope closer to 0 ITD.
results.evaluation: Claims C105-C113, C136, C139, C142-C143 are supported by intracellular recordings showing systematic changes in PSP amplitude and latency with sound level (Figure 8D-G). The quantitative measurements of latency slopes (C107) and the demonstration of cue interaction effects (C110-C113) are shown in Figure 8. However, the authors acknowledge limitations in the number of cells with exhaustive ITD/IID combinations (C146), which somewhat limits the generalizability of the findings.

results.result: The LSO is the primary nucleus for binaural processing of sound transients, with principal cells encoding spatial location based on temporal sensitivity and non-principal cells encoding location based on intensity. This represents a new view of brainstem binaural processing departing from traditional roles.
results.evaluation: Claims C10, C118-C120, C135, C159-C161, and C163 represent the main conclusions drawn from the experimental findings. These conclusions are supported by the convergence of evidence from in vivo recordings (superior ITD sensitivity in LSO vs MSO for clicks), in vitro experiments (requirement for synaptic inhibition), anatomical data (AIS inhibition), and computational modeling. The claim that this is the 'primary' nucleus (C10) is supported by the superior performance metrics compared to MSO for transient sounds.

results.result: Multiple specializations combine to enable LSO principal cells to process sound transients: exquisite timing in afferent inputs, fast intrinsic membrane properties, and strategic placement of inhibitory synapses on the AIS that enable one ear to veto the other over a narrow time window.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C7, C114-C116, C121-C122, C144-C145, and C157 synthesize the findings into a coherent mechanistic framework. These summary claims are supported by the convergence of evidence from multiple experimental approaches (in vivo recordings, in vitro experiments, anatomy, modeling). The 'vetoing mechanism' concept is well-supported by the data showing narrow windows of effective inhibition and the requirement for AIS synapses.

results.result: The temporal specializations in the LSO circuit evolved to support detection and lateralization of adventitious sounds generated by predator/prey movement, providing fast and reliable localization of sound transients.
results.evaluation: Claims C33, C127-C128, and C164 represent evolutionary and functional hypotheses that extend beyond the direct experimental evidence. While the data demonstrate superior temporal processing of transients in LSO (supporting C128), the evolutionary claims (C33, C127) rely on inference and speculation rather than direct evidence. The functional significance for predator/prey detection (C164) is plausible but speculative. These claims would require behavioral experiments or comparative studies across species to be fully supported.

results.result: The study used in vivo whole-cell patch clamp recordings from 19 LSO and 11 MSO neurons, and in vitro recordings from P19-22 gerbils. LSO neurons were classified as principal or non-principal based on established criteria.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C36, C46, and C79 describe the experimental methods and sample sizes. These are straightforward methodological statements supported by the Materials and Methods section. The sample sizes are adequate for the statistical analyses performed, though relatively small for some comparisons. The classification criteria (C46) are based on previous work by the same group.

results.result: ITD tuning in LSO neurons varies with sound level (steeper slopes and narrower functions at higher levels) and with characteristic frequency (narrower halfwidths at higher frequencies).
results.evaluation: Claims C49, C52, and C147 describe systematic variations in ITD tuning with stimulus parameters. These are supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 3 and correlation analysis (C52). The frequency dependence is explained by reference to glycine receptor distribution (C52), though this mechanistic explanation is speculative.

results.result: The AIS is a critical site for action potential initiation where inhibition can have outsized effects on neuronal output. Axo-axonic synapses are associated with brain disorders, but their physiological role has remained largely mysterious, particularly in cortex.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C14 and C156 provide background context supported by citations to previous literature. These are well-established facts in the field that motivate the current study. The claims accurately represent the state of knowledge about AIS function and the mystery surrounding axo-axonic synapses.

results.result: Background on binaural hearing: Locomotion generates adventitious sounds containing transients. Humans are sensitive to ITDs and IIDs. The classic duplex theory assigns ITD processing to MSO and IID processing to LSO, but LSO shows weak ITD sensitivity to most sounds except transients.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2, C16-C21, C23, C25-C32 provide background context supported by citations to previous literature. These accurately represent established knowledge in the field and prior observations that motivated the current study. The claims about adventitious sounds (C1, C2, C30-C32) are supported by behavioral studies in other species.

results.result: The inhibitory input to LSO neurons is provided by the MNTB and targets LSO somata, which makes the ineffectiveness of somatic inhibition simulation surprising.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C92 describe established anatomical connectivity supported by multiple citations. This background information motivates the surprising finding that somatic injection doesn't fully mimic synaptic inhibition, leading to the investigation of AIS synapses.

results.result: The EE interaction in MSO results in poorer ITD sensitivity to clicks than the IE interaction in LSO because transient stimuli cause suprathreshold monaural coincidences in MSO. In LSO's subtractive mechanism, strong monaural responses of opposite sign yield maximal binaural interaction.
results.evaluation: Claims C148-C153 provide mechanistic interpretation of the MSO versus LSO comparison. The explanation is supported by the data in Figure 3 and by citations to previous modeling work (C150). The logic is sound: MSO's multiplicative mechanism fails when monaural inputs are suprathreshold (C151), while LSO's subtractive mechanism benefits from strong monaural responses (C153).

results.result: The LSO circuit provides a model system for studying axo-axonic synapses with a clear physiological function (binaural sound localization), which may help understand such synapses elsewhere in the brain.
results.evaluation: Claims C154-C155 and C158 represent conclusions about the broader significance of the findings. The claim that this circuit is a good model system (C155) is supported by the clear functional role demonstrated (C154). However, the speculation about implications for other brain regions (C158) is more tentative and appropriately qualified with 'may help.'

results.result: The classical duplex account of LSO as an IID processor doesn't explain the extreme temporal specializations in the LSO circuit (including the calyx of Held), suggesting the LSO is specialized for temporal comparisons between ears.
results.evaluation: Claims C22, C24, C124-C126 present an argument based on inference from known anatomical features. The logic is sound: if LSO were simply an IID processor, the extreme temporal specializations would be unnecessary. This argument motivates the investigation of LSO's temporal processing capabilities. The claims are appropriately framed as inference rather than established fact.

results.result: Recent findings show that LSO principal cells have fast membrane properties and respond transiently to tones, underscoring the importance of timing in this circuit.
results.evaluation: Claims C34 and C129 cite previous work by the same group (Franken et al., 2018) that provides important context for the current findings. These claims accurately represent prior findings that complement the current study's focus on transient sound processing.

results.result: Background and limitations on IID-ITD interactions: ITD tuning curve centers suggest relative latencies of excitation and inhibition. IID-to-ITD conversion is complex for ongoing sounds but systematic for transients. The study has limited data on exhaustive ITD/IID combinations.
results.evaluation: Claims C59, C104, C108, C137-C138, C140-C141, and C146 provide context and acknowledge limitations. The inference about relative latencies (C59) is reasonable from the data. The background on IID-ITD interactions (C137-C138, C140) is supported by citations. The limitation (C146) is appropriately acknowledged by the authors.

results.result: MSO neurons are traditionally viewed as the ultimate ITD detectors and approach archetypal coincidence detectors, responding poorly to monaural stimulation and temporally misaligned inputs.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C69-C70 describe the traditional view of MSO function supported by citations to classic studies. These accurately represent established knowledge in the field and provide important context for the surprising finding that MSO shows poor ITD sensitivity to clicks.

results.result: Electrical shocks to LSO afferents are an appropriate analogue of acoustic clicks, as shown by previous in vitro and optogenetic studies. The effective window of inhibition is much smaller than IPSP duration, consistent with previous in vitro data.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C81 and C65 provide methodological justification and context supported by citations to previous studies. The claim that shocks are appropriate analogues of clicks (C80) is supported by the similarity of ITD sensitivity observed in vitro and in vivo (C81). The consistency with previous findings (C65) strengthens the current results.

results.result: Clarifications: The study doesn't claim LSO lacks IID sensitivity, only that it's temporally specialized for transients. Principal cells are the most numerous LSO cell type.
results.evaluation: Claims C134 and C162 provide important clarifications. C134 appropriately qualifies the study's conclusions to avoid overstating the case. C162 is supported by citations to anatomical studies and provides context for the claim that the time-based role is dominant.
